findings: FAIL reason 1, timing: only one half of the answer lands inside 30 seconds. The relative half ('Relative to JavaScript, yes, and quickly.') lands at 00:00:20,200, and its first number (18%) runs 00:00:23,117 to 00:00:29,133. Its end point (49%) runs 00:00:29,383 to 00:00:33,073, straddling the 30 s mark. The absolute half ('In raw numbers, though, JavaScript's lead grew...') starts at 00:00:33,323 and finishes at 00:00:42,006, outside the window. The first 20.2 s are the question plus a 16.5 s method sentence.

Why reason 1 matters: in ordinary English, 'catching up' means closing the gap, and on this count the gap more than doubled (1,147,998 to 2,454,635, and it grew in every single year). A viewer who leaves at 30 s leaves with 'yes, and quickly' and never hears the half that says no. VERDICT.md:352 requires the first 30 s to deliver what the title states; here they deliver the flattering half only.

FAIL reason 2, scope: the absolute half is stated with more generality than the data allows. On this count a developer is counted under every language in a repository they push to. Datasheet l.37 says 'a repository with a given programming language', and the file itself proves it: in 2026 Q1, summed over the same 92 economies, HTML has 5,689,786 pushers against JavaScript's 4,804,768, CSS has 4,548,919 and Dockerfile 1,417,124. So a TypeScript project that also holds JavaScript files (config files, for instance) adds to JavaScript's count, and 'JavaScript's lead' partly contains TypeScript projects. The narration discloses only the developer-level overlap ('a developer who pushes in both languages counts under each', at 00:01:31,135), not this repository-level rule, and only at 1:31.

Why reason 2 matters: GitHub's own Octoverse 2025, widely covered, says TypeScript overtook JavaScript and Python in August 2025 as #1 by monthly contributors (search, grade SNIPPET). A viewer who clicks a title that says 'on GitHub' and knows that headline hears 'JavaScript's lead grew' with nothing explaining the difference, and will conclude the video is wrong. It is not wrong on its count, but it does not say which count it uses.

Chart titles vs narration: s2, s3, s4, s5 and s6 match what is said and claim no more than the data supports. s1's title 'Developers who pushed to TypeScript and JavaScript repositories' reads as repositories whose main language is TypeScript or JavaScript, which overstates what is counted (see reason 2).

Chart/narration sync: the absolute sentence (0:33-0:42) is spoken over the ratio chart (frame at 37 s checked), which cannot show a gap. The pushers chart that shows the gap (end labels 4.80M and 2.35M) is on screen 0:00-0:20, when no number is spoken.

Checked and sound: 'the fastest growing was TypeScript' is explicitly scoped to the top 10 by pushers, and the chart marks reduced economy coverage for Dockerfile, Jupyter, Shell and C++. 'at most 5 percentage points in any earlier year' is true (max 4.54; the chart shows +4.5, the narration rounds up, so it understates the contrast). 'Economy by economy, the picture is the same' holds: the ratio rose in 92 of 92 economies and the absolute gap grew in 89 of 92. '47 of the 92' matches the histogram (31 + 14 + 2). 'The data shows how many developers pushed, not why' correctly declines to explain the 2025-26 jump.

Title and description: the title is a genuine question and the video answers it; no clickbait, no superlative, no thumbnail promise (no custom thumbnail exists). The description says what the data is and does not overclaim, but it does not state the counting rule either.

Would a viewer feel it delivered? A general viewer who stays to 0:42: yes. A developer who knows the Octoverse headline, which is the likely audience for this title in late 2026: not without the counting rule. Both required changes are small, and after them I would defend a PASS.
